## Proof

### 1. Setup and eigenvalue structure

Let $G$ be an undirected graph on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with edge set $\mathcal{E}$, and let $\mathcal{E}$ also include the implicit allowance of self-loops (i.e., the diagonal entries $P_{ii}$ are unconstrained in sign-pattern beyond $P_{ii}\ge 0$). We seek a matrix $P$ satisfying

$$
P_{ij}\ge 0,\quad P_{ij}=0\ \text{if }(i,j)\notin\mathcal{E},\quad P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1},\quad P=P^{T},
$$

that minimizes the mixing rate

$$
r(P)=\max\bigl\{|\lambda_2(P)|,\dots,|\lambda_n(P)|\bigr\},
$$

where $\lambda_1(P)=1\ge \lambda_2(P)\ge\cdots\ge \lambda_n(P)\ge -1$ are the real eigenvalues of $P$ (real because $P$ is symmetric).

Since $P$ is symmetric and stochastic, $P$ is doubly stochastic: $P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{1}^{T}P=\mathbf{1}^{T}$. Hence the uniform distribution $\pi=\tfrac1n\mathbf{1}$ is stationary, and $\mathbf{1}$ (normalized to $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\mathbf{1}$) is the eigenvector for $\lambda_1=1$. The remaining eigenvalues govern convergence to stationarity, and the mixing rate is exactly the spectral radius of $P$ restricted to the subspace $\mathbf{1}^{\perp}$.

### 2. Spectral characterization via a projection

Let $J=\tfrac1n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T}$ be the orthogonal projector onto $\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{1})$. Because $P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$ and $P=P^{T}$, the matrix $P$ commutes with $J$, and

$$
P = J + \bigl(P - J\bigr),
$$

where $P-J$ has eigenvalues $0,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n$ (the eigenvalue $1$ of $P$ is replaced by $0$). The mixing rate is therefore

$$
r(P) = \bigl\|P - J\bigr\|_2 = \max\bigl\{|\lambda_2|,\dots,|\lambda_n|\bigr\},
$$

the spectral norm (largest singular value) of $P-J$, which since $P-J$ is symmetric equals its largest eigenvalue in magnitude.

### 3. Convex reformulation as a semidefinite program

The constraint $r(P)\le r$ is equivalent to requiring every eigenvalue of $P-J$ to lie in $[-r,r]$, i.e.

$$
-r\,I \;\preceq\; P - J \;\preceq\; r\,I. \tag{$\star$}
$$

Indeed, $P-J$ is symmetric with spectrum $\{0,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n\}$, so $(\star)$ holds iff $\lambda_i\in[-r,r]$ for all $i\ge 2$, iff $r(P)\le r$.

All the remaining constraints are affine/linear in the entries of $P$:

- $P=P^{T}$: linear equalities $P_{ij}=P_{ji}$.
- $P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$: $n$ linear equalities $\sum_j P_{ij}=1$.
- $P_{ij}\ge 0$: linear inequalities.
- $P_{ij}=0$ for $(i,j)\notin\mathcal{E}$: linear equalities (fixing those entries to $0$).

The constraint $(\star)$ is a linear matrix inequality (LMI) in $(P,r)$, since $P-J$ is affine in $P$ and $rI$ is affine in $r$. Therefore the full problem

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\underset{P,\,r}{\text{minimize}}\quad & r \\
\text{subject to}\quad & P = P^{T}, \\
& P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}, \\
& P_{ij}\ge 0,\quad \forall\, i,j,\\
& P_{ij}=0,\quad \forall\,(i,j)\notin\mathcal{E},\\
& P - \tfrac1n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T} \preceq r\,I,\\
& P - \tfrac1n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T} \succeq -r\,I
\end{aligned}}\tag{SDP}
$$

is a **semidefinite program** (SDP): a convex optimization problem with a linear objective, linear equality/inequality constraints, and two linear matrix inequalities. The feasible set is convex (intersection of an affine subspace with the positive-semidefinite cone shifted by LMIs), and the objective is linear, so any local optimum is global.

### 4. Why this is the answer

Solving (SDP) — by an interior-point method, a spectral bundle method, or any SDP solver — yields the optimal value $r^\star$ and an optimal transition matrix $P^\star$. By construction:

- $P^\star$ satisfies all four Markov-chain constraints (non-negativity, graph support, stochasticity, symmetry).
- $r^\star = r(P^\star) = \max_{i\ge 2}|\lambda_i(P^\star)|$ is the smallest achievable mixing rate over all symmetric stochastic matrices supported on $G$.

The equivalence established in §2–§3 is exact: $r(P)\le r \iff (\star)$, so minimizing $r$ over the feasible set of Markov chains is *precisely* minimizing $r$ subject to $(\star)$, with no relaxation or gap. Hence $P^\star$ is the global minimizer of the mixing rate.

### 5. Remarks on structure (not required for correctness)

- The diagonal $P_{ii}$ is free (self-loops are allowed), which is essential: without self-loops the problem can be infeasible for bipartite graphs (a bipartite graph forces $\lambda_n=-1$ for any stochastic $P$ without self-loops, giving $r=1$). Allowing $P_{ii}\ge 0$ lets the SDP "lazily" stay at a node, shrinking $|\lambda_n|$ and improving mixing.
- When $G$ is regular of degree $d$, a natural feasible point is the simple random walk $P_{ij}=1/d$ for $(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}$, but it is generally **not** optimal; the SDP exploits self-loops and non-uniform edge weights to reduce $r$ further.
- The dual of (SDP) provides a certificate of optimality (a pair of dual PSD matrices bounding $r^\star$ from below), so the solution is verifiable.

### Conclusion

The transition probability matrix $P$ of the symmetric Markov chain on $G$ that minimizes the mixing rate $r$ is obtained as the solution of the semidefinite program (SDP) above: minimize $r$ subject to the stochastic/symmetry/support constraints and the two linear matrix inequalities $-rI\preceq P-\tfrac1n\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T}\preceq rI$. This SDP is convex, its optimum is global, and its solution $P^\star$ achieves the smallest possible second-largest-eigenvalue-in-magnitude among all feasible symmetric stochastic matrices supported on the graph.
